In summary, our research is concerned with
a quantitative measure of the amount of confidential data which may be revealed by a program.
the analysis of the leakage of confidential information by programs written in an imperative language, and the design of techniques to prevent such leakage.
the analysis and design of programs which are secure against leakage of confidential data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no way in which the amount of confidential data which may be leaked can be reduced by more than 1 bit by the use of if statements and equality tests.
equality tests and if-statements do not leak information.
the leakage of confidential information by programs in the language considered is not only possible, but inevitable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the analysis is not only useful in its own right but also provides a good basis for the design of a more efficient analysis.
the analysis is sound, complete and efficient, and that it can be applied to a large class of programs.
it is possible to write programs which do not leak information, but that it is very difficult to do so.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the amount of confidential leakage is not a function of the length of a program, but of the number of equality tests and if-statements in the program.
, in order to prevent leakage, one should avoid equality testing and conditional execution.
the amount of confidential data which may be leaked is often much less than one might have expected, even when programs are written with the intention of leaking as much information as possible.
